## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design runtime attestation bridging CI and runtime, using SPIFFE/mTLS, OPA, and per-tenant revocation. Evaluates trade-offs around performance, key management, and revocation latency.

## Key Concepts

- Runtime attestation evidence (image digest, SBOM hash, runtime state)
- Attestation service with mutual TLS and SPIFFE identities
- Admission control with OPA to gate scheduling
- Per-tenant revocation and key rotation for attestations
- Testing in a single namespace before broader rollout

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: attestation-agent
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: agent
        image: example/attestation-agent:latest
        env:
        - name: ATTESTATION_ENDPOINT
          value: https://attestor.default.svc.cluster.local
        - name: CERT_FILE
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: attestation-cert
              key: tls.crt
        - name: KEY_FILE
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: attestation-cert
              key: tls.key
```

- How would you scale attestation for thousands of CNFs without adding startup latency?
- How would you handle revocation propagation when an attacker signs a new image at runtime?

## Why This Is Asked
This question validates the ability to design per-tenant request mutation with runtime configuration, isolation, and safe rollback—a realistic pattern in CNF gateways deploying WASM filters.

## Key Concepts
- WASM sandboxing and module loading in a CNF sidecar
- Tenant-scoped policy storage with fast reloads via ConfigMap
- Validation, rollback, and observability in a live gateway
- End-to-end testing using a one-namespace manifest

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf.filter.rules
  namespace: cnf-gateway
data:
  rules.json: |
    {
      "tenant1:abc123": {
        "pathRewrite": {
          "pattern": "^/v1/(.*)$",
          "replacement": "/tenant1/v1/$1"
        },
        "headers": {
          "add": {
            "X-Forwarded-Tenant": "tenant1",
            "X-Tenant-ID": "tenant1"
          }
        }
      }
    }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: cnf-gateway
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: cnf-gateway
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cnf-gateway
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: cnf-gateway
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: cnf-gateway
      containers:
      - name: proxy
        image: envoyproxy/envoy:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: wasm-filter
          mountPath: /etc/wasm-filters
        - name: rules
          mountPath: /etc/config
        env:
        - name: CONFIG_MAP_NAME
          value: cnf.filter.rules
      volumes:
      - name: wasm-filter
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: rules
        configMap:
          name: cnf.filter.rules
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design tenant-isolated traffic experiments, balancing fidelity with safety. Requires practical knowledge of service meshes, per-tenant config, and data privacy in production-like environments.

## Key Concepts
- Traffic shadowing with Istio or similar mesh
- Per-tenant config via NamespaceConfigMap
- Tenant selection via request header X-TENANT-ID
- Isolation: staging sink in separate trust domain
- Validation: one-namespace manifest and observability hooks

## Code Example
```yaml
# VirtualService skeleton showing mirror usage
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: tenant-shadow
spec:
  hosts:
  - prod-svc
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-tenant-id:
          exact: "<tenant-id>"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: prod-svc
    - weight: 100
    mirror:
      host: staging-svc
      subset: v1
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you scale per-tenant shadow percentages with burst traffic?
- How do you monitor shadow traffic to ensure no PII leakage or data exposure?

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests the ability to design multi-tenant upgrade workflows with strict rollback mechanisms and metric-driven canary promotion—a common production CNF pattern at scale.

- Safe rollback capabilities with idempotent manifests

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: cnf.example/v1
kind: TenantUpgradePolicy
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-upgrade
spec:
  tenantId: tenant-a
  targetVersion: v2.1.0
  canaryTrafficPercent: 5
  promotionCriteria:
    latencyThresholdMs: 100
    errorRateThresholdPercent: 0.5
    observationWindowMinutes: 10
  rollbackConfig:
    autoRollbackOnFailure: true
    maxRetries: 3
```
